sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe exclusion and sanction concepts, including the purpose of exclusion lists, who maintains them, and how exclusions are imposed and removed.
- Recognize billing prohibitions that prevent payment for items or services furnished, ordered, or prescribed by excluded individuals or entities, and the practice's duty to screen employees, contractors, and vendors.
- Report compliance concerns through proper channels, including the compliance officer, chain of command, hotlines, and government authorities, while staying within the assistant's scope of practice.
- Apply safety and escalation principles so that potential exclusions, improper billing, and other compliance concerns are flagged promptly, objectively, and confidentially.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Being excluded is like being banned from a club you are not allowed back into until you are formally invited back.

### Question 2

The OIG is like the referee who keeps the official list of players who are not allowed in the game.

### Question 3

Exclusion is like removing a broken playground swing so no one gets hurt and nothing gets damaged.

### Question 4

Medicare and Medicaid are like the big public clubs the government runs; being excluded means you cannot join those clubs.

### Question 5

Both a single player and a whole team can be banned from the league.

### Question 6

A driver's license and a library card are different cards from different places; losing one does not always mean losing the other.

### Question 7

Some rules are automatic like a red light you must stop at, while other rules are up to the referee to decide.

### Question 8

Committing fraud is like cheating in a big game; the referee removes you so you cannot cheat again.

### Question 9

Hurting someone in your care is a reason to be removed so others stay safe.

### Question 10

Being unbanned is not automatic; you have to ask to come back and get a yes first.

### Question 11

You check the weather before a trip and keep checking in case it changes, rather than looking once and never again.

### Question 12

Everyone who could touch the billing or care, like employees and vendors, gets checked, not just one group.

### Question 13

Besides being banned, you might also have to pay money for breaking the rules.

### Question 14

It is like checking more than one wanted list so you do not miss a name on a different one.

### Question 15

Debarment is like being blocked from bidding on school projects, which is different from being banned from a health club.

### Question 16

OIG is short for the Office of Inspector General, the watchdog office.

### Question 17

If the person who writes the order is banned, the program will not pay for what they ordered.

### Question 18

If a banned person does the work, the program will not pay for that work.

### Question 19

Billing for a banned person is like submitting a fake receipt; it can get you in serious trouble.

### Question 20

If you think a name is on the no-entry list, tell a grown-up in charge and do not send the bill.

### Question 21

Two different people can have the same name, so you check more details before deciding they are the same person.

### Question 22

Even if the banned player is not the one scoring, having them on the team can still break the rules.

### Question 23

Being banned also means you cannot secretly run the business from behind the scenes.

### Question 24

The team that wants to play in the big game has to check that its own players are allowed.

### Question 25

If you see something wrong, tell the trusted person in charge through the right way, not by shouting it around.

### Question 26

If you honestly tell about a problem, you should not get in trouble just for speaking up.

### Question 27

Good faith means you speak up because you honestly think something is wrong, not to hurt anyone.

### Question 28

The False Claims Act is like a rule that punishes people who turn in fake bills and protects those who report them.

### Question 29

If you find a mistake on a bill, stop sending more and tell the person in charge.

### Question 30

If you were paid for something that was against the rules, you give the money back.

### Question 31

The hotline is like a special phone line where you can quietly tell the referee about cheating.

### Question 32

Write down only what you really saw, like a referee noting facts, not guessing or name-calling.

### Question 33

Your job is to tell the person in charge, not to play detective or judge.

### Question 34

A compliance program is like a set of safety rules that stop mistakes before they happen and fix them if they do.

### Question 35

A good safety plan has written rules, teaches everyone, and gives a private way to speak up.

### Question 36

You can often raise your hand without everyone knowing it was you, so you feel safe telling the truth.

### Question 37

Secrets about an investigation stay private, shared only with people who truly need to know.

### Question 38

If you see smoke, you call for help right away, not next year.

### Question 39

You tell the person the rulebook says to tell first, then go higher if needed.

### Question 40

Recording a bigger job than you really did is like claiming a bigger score than you earned.

### Question 41

Taking secret money to send patients somewhere is against the rules, so you tell the person in charge.

### Question 42

The anti-kickback rule stops people from trading money or gifts to send patients a certain way.

### Question 43

A whistleblower is like a helper who points out cheating and may get a reward if the team wins the case.

### Question 44

Sending a bill for something that never happened is like charging for a toy you never sold.

### Question 45

If you keep finding the same mistake, you tell the person in charge so they can fix the root cause.

### Question 46

Even a real, well-done job cannot be paid if the person who did it was banned.

### Question 47

You check the safety list often, not once every ten years, so you catch new names quickly.

### Question 48

Keeping a record of your checks is like keeping your homework to show you did it.

### Question 49

You wait for the official welcome-back letter before treating someone as allowed again.

### Question 50

If you lose your driver's license, you might also lose permission to drive for the big delivery program.

### Question 51

A permissive rule is like a referee who may or may not call a penalty depending on the situation.

### Question 52

Besides the national no-entry list, your state may keep its own list you also need to check.

### Question 53

If a supplier is banned, you stop buying from them for the big program and tell the person in charge.

### Question 54

If you realize you took money you should not have, the honest move is to give it back and tell the right people.

### Question 55

A hotline is a private phone you can use to quietly tell about a problem without saying who you are.

### Question 56

If a grown-up asks you to do something against the rules, you say no and tell a higher-up.

### Question 57

Do not rip up or change the papers; leave them alone and tell the right person.

### Question 58

Whistleblower protection is like a shield that keeps you safe for honestly pointing out a problem.

### Question 59

If you are not sure something is wrong, you still tell a grown-up so they can check.

### Question 60

Getting in trouble just for telling the truth is against the rules.

### Question 61

The compliance officer is like the safety captain who makes sure rules are followed and handles reports.

### Question 62

If the person you would normally tell is the one doing wrong, tell their boss or use the private hotline.

### Question 63

The list is like a guest list you check to see who is allowed in before you pay them.

### Question 64

Hiring a banned player can cost your team money as a penalty.

### Question 65

You cannot sneak a banned player in with a fake name or a middleman; the rules still apply.

### Question 66

You check the guest list before letting someone in, not a year later.

### Question 67

The office checks its own guest list even if the club also checks at the door.

### Question 68

Tell the facts you saw, not rumors you heard or what you personally think about the person.

### Question 69

Serious cheating in the big public programs gets reported to the official referee, not the newspaper.

### Question 70

You must ask and get a yes to come back; the door does not open by itself.

### Question 71

Upcoding is like writing a bigger number on the score sheet than you actually earned.

### Question 72

Writing down what really happened is like keeping a receipt that proves what you did.

### Question 73

Code the real work that is written down, not the biggest number you can imagine.

### Question 74

If the receipt is missing, you find it before charging, not guess what was bought.

### Question 75

Program integrity is like keeping the game fair by catching cheaters and stopping waste.

### Question 76

The team is responsible for checking its own players, not the players or the fans.

### Question 77

You re-check the list on a schedule, like a monthly safety check, not just once.

### Question 78

If you see a maybe-banned name on a bill, stop and check before sending it.

### Question 79

Speaking up about problems is part of the job of keeping people safe and honest.

### Question 80

Being banned affects getting paid by the big public programs, not everything in your personal life.

### Question 81

When you are not sure where to go, check the rulebook or ask the safety captain.

### Question 82

Before paying a new player, check they are actually allowed on the team.

### Question 83

When the referee comes to check, the team captain handles it and everyone cooperates.

### Question 84

If someone asks you to help tell a big lie on a bill, you say no and tell the right person.

### Question 85

Your job is to notice, follow the rules, and tell the right people, not to be the judge.
